materials.text:
Now that you are holding onto a Node you have a few responsibilities:

First, you must read from the Node.Ready() channel and process the updates
it contains. These steps may be performed in parallel, except as noted in step
2.

1. Write HardState, Entries, and Snapshot to persistent storage if they are
not empty. Note that when writing an Entry with Index i, any
previously-persisted entries with Index >= i must be discarded.

2. Send all Messages to the nodes named in the To field. It is important that
no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk,
and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while
entries from the same batch are being persisted). To reduce the I/O latency, an
optimization can be applied to make leader write to disk in parallel with its
followers (as explained at section 10.2.1 in Raft thesis). If any Message has type
MsgSnap, call Node.ReportSnapshot() after it has been sent (these messages may be
large).

Note: Marshalling messages is not thread-safe; it is important that you
make sure that no new entries are persisted while marshalling.
The easiest way to achieve this is to serialize the messages directly inside
your main raft loop.

3. Apply Snapshot (if any) and CommittedEntries to the state machine.
If any committed Entry has Type EntryConfChange, call Node.ApplyConfChange()
to apply it to the node. The configuration change may be cancelled at this point
by setting the NodeID field to zero before calling ApplyConfChange
(but ApplyConfChange must be called one way or the other, and the decision to cancel
must be based solely on the state machine and not external information such as
the observed health of the node).

4. Call Node.Advance() to signal readiness for the next batch of updates.
This may be done at any time after step 1, although all updates must be processed
in the order they were returned by Ready.

Second, all persisted log entries must be made available via an
implementation of the Storage interface. The provided MemoryStorage
type can be used for this (if you repopulate its state upon a
restart), or you can supply your own disk-backed implementation.

Third, when you receive a message from another node, pass it to Node.Step:

	func recvRaftRPC(ctx context.Context, m raftpb.Message) {
		n.Step(ctx, m)
	}

Finally, you need to call Node.Tick() at regular intervals (probably
via a time.Ticker). Raft has two important timeouts: heartbeat and the
election timeout. However, internally to the raft package time is
represented by an abstract "tick".

The encoded closed_joint_cycle=true therefore violates the assertion that this admitted operation must not reach that cycle. The previous artifact sampled the lossy Status copy; this correction answers the exact observation issue without changing inputs or weakening the requirement.

The scheduler drains its local queue and requires HasReady=false at each capture. materials.text:
Now that you are holding onto a Node you have a few responsibilities:

First, you must read from the Node.Ready() channel and process the updates
it contains. These steps may be performed in parallel, except as noted in step
2.

1. Write HardState, Entries, and Snapshot to persistent storage if they are
not empty. Note that when writing an Entry with Index i, any
previously-persisted entries with Index >= i must be discarded.

2. Send all Messages to the nodes named in the To field. It is important that
no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk,
and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while
entries from the same batch are being persisted). To reduce the I/O latency, an
optimization can be applied to make leader write to disk in parallel with its
followers (as explained at section 10.2.1 in Raft thesis). If any Message has type
MsgSnap, call Node.ReportSnapshot() after it has been sent (these messages may be
large).

Note: Marshalling messages is not thread-safe; it is important that you
make sure that no new entries are persisted while marshalling.
The easiest way to achieve this is to serialize the messages directly inside
your main raft loop.

3. Apply Snapshot (if any) and CommittedEntries to the state machine.
If any committed Entry has Type EntryConfChange, call Node.ApplyConfChange()
to apply it to the node. The configuration change may be cancelled at this point
by setting the NodeID field to zero before calling ApplyConfChange
(but ApplyConfChange must be called one way or the other, and the decision to cancel
must be based solely on the state machine and not external information such as
the observed health of the node).

4. Call Node.Advance() to signal readiness for the next batch of updates.
This may be done at any time after step 1, although all updates must be processed
in the order they were returned by Ready.

Second, all persisted log entries must be made available via an
implementation of the Storage interface. The provided MemoryStorage
type can be used for this (if you repopulate its state upon a
restart), or you can supply your own disk-backed implementation.

Third, when you receive a message from another node, pass it to Node.Step:

	func recvRaftRPC(ctx context.Context, m raftpb.Message) {
		n.Step(ctx, m)
	}

Finally, you need to call Node.Tick() at regular intervals (probably
via a time.Ticker). Raft has two important timeouts: heartbeat and the
election timeout. However, internally to the raft package time is
represented by an abstract "tick".

formation.explanation: A leader assigns entry term/index, replicates and counts Match acknowledgements through active voter quorums. Current-term matching gates commit advancement. Followers match the preceding entry and reject committed-prefix conflicts; Ready exposes committed work to the caller. Node serializes Step/Tick/configuration work; RawNode instead requires caller serialization. Duplicate votes are ignored, learners are excluded from tally counts, and active joint voter sets decide elections and commits. Rejections use log conflict hints; heartbeat responses unpause replication, with snapshots used when compacted history is unavailable. Application observes ordered committed entries and independently installs configurations.

context.explanation: Campaign and term handling acquire or lose leader authority. Real candidacy increments term; reset discards peer support and readOnly tracking. A new leader retains history, appends an empty current-term entry and conservatively delays configuration proposals until prior history is applied. Campaign admission scans for unapplied committed configuration entries and requires voter eligibility with no pending snapshot. A pre-vote victory starts a real campaign, and a vote victory becomes leader. Lease/check-quorum policy can suppress disruption; transfer catches up a voter before TimeoutNow, with timed abort. Old-term network replies are filtered before role dispatch; same-term leader traffic makes candidates followers. Restart reconstructs configuration/history and starts follower.

connection.explanation: Progress support is leader-context local, while committed history survives reset. Configuration application changes quorum interpretation and can itself advance commit. Persistence-qualified replies connect durable history to election and append support; old-term storage completion cannot discard potentially overwritten unstable entries. Joint configuration retains both voter sets until leave-joint; quorum decisions require both majorities. Committed snapshots are term-independent but obsolete snapshots are rejected. Ready completion advances a local applied marker consumed by campaign admission, while ApplyConfChange separately installs membership. Safe-read acknowledgements are cleared by reset, whereas pre-current-term pending reads survive in a separate slice; later append-driven first commit releases them under the then-current context. ReadIndex callers must tolerate loss and retry.

items.rationale:
Applicability: the accepted v1 claim and bindings assign implicit joint departure to Raft when possible (S-joint-contract and S-joint-flag). The fixed input explicitly chooses JointImplicit; it does not reinterpret explicit joint mode or impose a ten-tick completion deadline. The entering change is applied before Advance, so the separate paused early-Advance dispute does not apply. History: the fixed harness creates the declared three-voter initial snapshot, elects node 1 using implementation-generated messages, persists each Ready before sends, and commits removal of node 3 at index 3 in term 2. It applies that configuration, requests transfer to voter 2 before completing the same Ready, then completes Advance. This is serialized public RawNode activity with no forged acknowledgements. One generated TimeoutNow is dropped during the transfer attempt; every message and every Ready is processed in the later suffix. Actual admission records applied=3, transfer_clear=true and the original leader, with no omitted application callback.

Observation/correlation: fixed corrected lines 121-122 read active raft.trk.Config.AutoLeave and outgoing voters under exclusive single-thread ownership; Status only supplies its unaffected scalar fields and a separate status_auto_leave diagnostic. The active_result event is correlated to admitted by scenario, leader=1 and joint_index=3, independent of compared state values. Current run 30c25f44a82b4d0c81c3b3b6e2d9d883 exited 0, reported cycle_equal=true, active auto_leave=true, joint=true, transfer_clear=true, no leave proposals in the cycle or total, and applied=commit=3. I reconstructed split Go JSON output chunks and independently compared the two retained 8915-character state strings: they are identical. The encoded closed_joint_cycle=true therefore violates the assertion that this admitted operation must not reach that cycle. The previous artifact sampled the lossy Status copy; this correction answers the exact observation issue without changing inputs or weakening the requirement.

Recurrence and endpoint: recursive capture covers all three RawNodes, raft state, term/vote/roles, fixed configuration, peer progress/inflight arrays, timers, pending reads/messages, complete log/storage values, unstable state and saved Ready completion steps. The scheduler drains its local queue and requires HasReady=false at each capture. It repeats the same ordered Tick-all/drain schedule for a full ten-tick period and checks roles and term after ticks and protocol mutations. No goroutines, external callbacks or pending client work exist. Logger output, unused trace logger, single-thread MemoryStorage mutex and monotonic call instrumentation are excluded; S-storage-state shows counters only increment and are never used for a storage decision. Slice capacity/pointer identity do not affect this no-append heartbeat cycle. Function entry identities plus the recursively captured receiver state determine callbacks here. The global RNG is not sampled in this suffix: resetRandomizedElectionTimeout is reached through role/term reset, while the fixed unchanged roles and frequent heartbeat delivery keep followers below election timeout. Thus this is a repeatable closed protocol suffix, not an inference of infinite stalling from a finite wait. The source corroborates the missing trigger: only appliedTo attempts leave; transfer abort clears a field, and an idle heartbeat suffix produces no further application completion.

Completion/counterevidence: a separately tagged client rescue after the principal result generates one leave proposal and finishes at applied=commit=5 with joint=false. This shows a later stimulus can rescue the transition, but the caller is not required to issue it for an implicit transition. All generated work drains before normal successful return. The observation supports the scoped lost automatic continuation, not failure under every schedule or consensus safety loss.

The fixed v1 harness for O-status-auto-fidelity creates the permitted one-voter initial snapshot, elects through real self-vote persistence/Advance, and proposes an implicit joint learner addition. No active flag is injected or mutated by the test. The committed entry at index 3 is passed to ApplyConfChange; switchToConfig installs its tracker before returning ConfState, whose AutoLeave is independently copied by ProgressTracker.ConfState (S-confstate-export). Thus the installed event supplies an actual true expected value, not a hardcoded desired output. The next operation is public RawNode.Status, with no intervening protocol mutation and exclusive single-thread ownership.

The fixed monitor selects status_result and correlates it with installed using scenario, node=1 and entry_index=3; these are independent identity fields. Applicability selects the declared implicit input and its actually installed true flag. The assertion directly compares observed_auto_leave against installed.expected_auto_leave. Run cf49d6a54dac42d187e53cbec83f0ea8 completed with exit 0 and records expected=true, live=true, observed=false, outgoing_count=1. This is a complete local value-copy counterexample: getStatus uses Config.Clone, and the returned literal omits AutoLeave. The current-status and copy contracts apply to this field; no external caller action is necessary to establish value fidelity.

After observation, the harness finishes Advance and drains the generated automatic leave. Cleanup records has_ready=false and applied=commit=4 with live_auto_leave=false. There are no goroutines or pending local callbacks to join. Learner-bound traffic was dropped under the declared transport policy; it is not voting support and does not corrupt the self-quorum history. The successful later exit is contrary to any inference of active-state corruption, but does not repair the earlier incorrect snapshot. Scope remains public Status configuration fidelity, not Status.MarshalJSON contents, a failed transition, or a consensus-safety consequence.
